events.text:
⚡️🇺🇸🇷🇺🇮🇷 — CIA Director John Ratcliffe used a rare, unannounced visit to Moscow this week to warn Russian officials against any escalatory action against NATO allies — particularly Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania — and to press Russia to reduce military and economic support for Iran, according to Politico.
➡️ The trip marked the first known visit to Moscow by a CIA director under Trump. The C-17 military plane that flew Ratcliffe into the Russian capital took off from Latvia, according to flight-tracking data. A source said the meeting was "primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states."
➡️ Ratcliffe also raised Iran, conveying a desire for Moscow to stop sharing weapons and defense technology with Tehran and advising against "overreacting" if affected by expanded U.S. sanctions. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday threatened significantly broader sanctions on countries refusing to cut economic ties with Iran. Russia has reportedly shipped material to Iran for its drone arsenal and may be helping Tehran target U.S. facilities.
➡️ Trump described the visit as "semi-routine" but acknowledged it was about ending the war: "I hate to disappoint people. We would like to see the war with Ukraine end." Ratcliffe is generally viewed as a hawk on Russia, and the trip marks the latest instance of Trump deploying his CIA director to navigate tense diplomacy with major adversaries — following a secret visit to Cuba in May. The visit comes amid intensifying Russian strikes on Ukraine and threats against NATO countries, sparking fears of aggressive hybrid warfare or limited military action against allies, including the UK.
⭐️ Follow

events.text:
🚨🇷🇺 Russia's Submarine Built To Launch Poseidon Nuclear Drones Begins Sea Trials
Russia’s Project 09851 Khabarovsk special-purpose nuclear submarine appears to have begun its first factory sea trials after being photographed leaving Severodvinsk on August 17. The voyage takes Russia’s first submarine designed from the outset around the Poseidon underwater weapon from shipyard construction into at-sea testing.
🔸 Khabarovsk was laid down at Sevmash on July 27, 2014. It was rolled out of its construction hall on November 1, 2025, and physically lowered into the water later that month before undergoing final outfitting and dockside tests.
🔸 Russia’s Defense Ministry said the submarine was built to deploy modern underwater weapons, including robotic systems. Its detailed specifications remain classified, but it is widely assessed to carry up to six Poseidon vehicles.
🔸 Poseidon is an autonomous, nuclear-powered and nuclear-capable underwater drone designed to travel across intercontinental distances. Instead of flying through the radar and interceptor networks built to detect ballistic missiles, it approaches its target beneath the ocean.
🔸 In October 2025, President Vladimir Putin announced that Russia had launched a Poseidon from a carrier submarine and activated its onboard nuclear reactor for the first time. The vehicle then operated under its own nuclear power for a period of time, demonstrating that the system had progressed beyond launch-only testing.
🔸 The challenge for the United States begins before Poseidon even enters the water. Preventing a launch would require the U.S. Navy to locate and continuously track Khabarovsk across an enormous ocean area without losing contact with the submarine.
🔸 Once released, Poseidon creates a separate detection problem. American forces would have to find and follow a fast, deep-running autonomous vehicle traveling along an unpredictable underwater route that existing missile-defense interceptors cannot cover.
🔸 Russia already operates Belgorod, a converted Oscar-class submarine accepted by the Navy in 2022 and used as the first Poseidon carrier. Khabarovsk is more significant because it is the first submarine designed from the keel up specifically to deploy the weapon.
Khabarovsk must still complete factory and state trials before entering service, but its first voyage marks the transition from construction to an active sea-testing program. Once commissioned, it would give Russia a dedicated platform capable of delivering strategic nuclear weapons along ocean routes outside the architecture of U.S. missile defense.
Does the U.S. have any realistic way to stop Poseidon once Khabarovsk launches it?

events.text: Aftermath in occupied Donetsk shows extensive damage after a missile and drone strike. Local reports say about 13 impacts hit Russian military sites, including a former research institute, used as a troop deployment site and headquarters. An underground parking complex reportedly used to shelter launchers and armored vehicles was hit by at least 6 missiles.

events.title: Telegram
events.text: At least 7 missile hits were recorded in occupied Donetsk. Reports say missiles penetrated an underground parking garage where a Russian command post was allegedly located. Nearby streets were closed while survivors were evacuated. Missile fragments were recovered, but the weapon has not been identified. It could be a small cruise missile, ERAM or even a glide bomb (Vyrivniuvach).

events.text: Ukraine's Apex border guard drone unit says its FPV drones are operating on Russian territory. During the latest mission, operators detected and struck a Russian self-propelled artillery system that Russian forces had been using to provide fire support to their units.

events.title: Telegram
events.text: Russia has converted up to 17 S-400 launchers to strike Ukraine with RM-48U guided missiles, according to Ukraine's HUR. Five special missile groups are deployed in Russia's Bryansk and Rostov regions. Russia used about 15 RM-48Us per month from January through June, but fired 46 in the first 20 days of July. HUR estimates Russia has around 400 missiles in stock and plans to produce up to 500 more in 2026.

events.title: Telegram
events.text:
China has become a key supply link for Russia's Shahed drones, WSJ reports. Ukrainian experts found turbojet engines from China's Telefly in newer variants that can reach about 480 km/h, roughly three times the speed of older models. Ukraine usually intercepts more than 90% of older Shaheds, but officials say the jet versions can outrun interceptor drones, forcing the use of fighters or scarce air defense missiles.
Ukrainian specialists are also finding more Chinese antennas, modems, SIM cards, servos and gyroscopes in Shaheds as Western components decline. WSJ reports that many US and European parts previously reached Iran and Russia through intermediaries and shell companies in mainland China and Hong Kong.

events.text: Ukraine's HUR published an interactive 3D model of Russia's Su-35S fighter and data on 79 companies involved in its production, saying 22 remain unsanctioned by any country in the sanctions coalition. The firms are involved in engines, fuel systems, controls, communications, guidance, electronic warfare systems and missiles used by the aircraft. HUR named Rubin, Gidroavtomatika and the Oktava research institute among the companies that remain unsanctioned.

events.text:
🤔 Mysterious funeral wreaths appear at HQs of European weapons firms serving Ukraine
The elaborate black and white-accented floral arrangements were accompanied by portraits of RSI Europe CEO Tomas Milasaukas and David Chour — executive director of the Czechoslovak Group arms concern.
The first wreath was spotted on the grounds of an industrial park near Vilnius, Lithuania, where RSI Europe is based. The ribbons carried the notes "Forever in our hearts" and "From close friends." Another wreath was placed at the entrance to Czechoslovak Group's Prague HQ, with the phrase "in loving memory" emblazoned on its ribbon in Czech.
💬 As far as we know, both men are alive and in good health. It's unclear who made and distributed the wreaths, but we can take a guess as to why:
RSI Europe has profited handsomely from NATO's proxy war against Russia in Ukraine, delivering EW-resistant FPV drones and remote detonation systems to Kiev and promising to integrate computer vision and AI in the near future. RSI Europe reported $18 million in revenues in 2025.
The Czechoslovak Group is an even bigger fish, manufacturing 105, 120, and 155mm ammunition, propulsion systems, and heavy ground equipment, and generating over $650 million in earnings from its Ukraine contracts in the first half of 2026 alone.
The pair are just two pieces of a puzzle that includes hundreds of European companies — big and small — involved in the war.
Russia's Ministry of Defense published the addresses of some of these European defense companies in April, Moscow's clearest warning yet that the sites would be targeted if the crisis escalates.
For now, the alliance is hiding behind its Article 5 guarantees, shipping all manner of defense production to Ukraine as[ Russian drones and missiles ](https://t.me/geopolitics_prime/73625)make weapons manufacturing and military logistics there impossible to maintain.
